sections.title: Foreword

summary.text: The foreword, by WHO Assistant Director-General Timothy Evans, states that sound ethical standards are an essential part of health research and that WHO is stepping up efforts to ensure they are met, especially in resource-poor settings where local researchers and ethics committees must be able to recognise and handle ethical issues. It explains that the casebook, developed under the lead of WHO's Ethics Review Committee, uses cases based on real studies for individual reading or group discussion as an effective way to learn to apply ethical principles.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the casebook's 64 case studies, each built around one or two ethical problems in planning, reviewing or conducting health research, and intended mainly for teaching researchers and research ethics committee members, especially in international settings. The cases are short, grouped by main issue and drawn from real projects, with names, dates and places changed so that readers concentrate on the dilemmas. It also explains WHO's reasons for the book, including the educational work of its Research Ethics Review Committee and the case-based workshops held with the Harvard School of Public Health since 1999, which found that discussing cases helps limit cultural bias and leads to concrete responses.

sections.title: Teaching Guide

summary.text: A teaching guide for facilitators who use the casebook in courses and workshops on research ethics. It first covers the method of case-based teaching, stressing the facilitator's role in guiding active discussion among participants and remaining open to cases with no single right answer instead of steering towards a preferred conclusion. It then reviews the main issues raised in each chapter and suggests discussion questions, ending with themes such as how scientific misconduct should be defined, judged and reported. A short list of further resources on teaching with case studies closes the section.

sections.title: The Case Studies
Chapter I Defining “Research”

summary.text: Opens Chapter I, which asks what counts as 'research' and therefore when a research ethics committee's approval must be sought. It separates research, whose main purpose is to produce new knowledge, from medical treatment meant to benefit an individual patient and from activities such as surveillance, audit or quality improvement. The introduction warns that the pursuit of knowledge must not outweigh participants' welfare, recalling the Nazi experiments and noting risks such as the therapeutic misconception and harms from sensitive social research. It closes with suggested readings, including CDC guidance on telling public health research from non-research and an article on distinguishing audit from research.

sections.title: Case 1. SARS and airplane passengers

summary.text: Case 1 describes a national public health centre that, during the 2003 SARS outbreak, traced airline passengers who had flown with suspected cases and asked for blood samples and medical histories from healthy travellers, even though delays meant testing came after the likely incubation period. It asks whether the data were collected for surveillance, disease prevention or research, and whether ethics committee approval and informed consent were needed.

sections.title: Case 2. Evaluating sexual health and family planning programmes

summary.text: Case 2 describes an institute running three donor-funded prevention projects in developing countries, covering HIV testing and counselling for adolescents, prenatal care with HIV partner notification, and a condom programme that sanctions brothel owners, each with a required evaluation. The institute argues that these low-risk operations evaluations need no ethics review, and the questions ask what separates research from programme evaluation, whether oversight is needed and how risk bears on review.

sections.title: Case 3. A treatment for central nervous system conditions

summary.text: Case 3 describes a neurosurgeon in an Asian city who has treated over 500 patients with ALS, Parkinson's disease, stroke and paralysis by injecting olfactory cells from aborted fetuses, calling it innovative therapy. He reports stabilization and better quality of life based on videos and a patient survey but refuses placebo-controlled or sham-surgery trials, saying they would harm suffering patients. The questions ask whether this is therapy, experiment or research, whether a placebo trial would be unethical, how effectiveness could otherwise be shown and who should monitor physicians.

sections.title: Case 4. Documenting the health conditions of an indigenous community

summary.text: Case 4 describes a university team asked, under a tight three-month funding deadline, to document the health of an isolated indigenous community in South America, which begins survey work and a photographic database while its blood sampling and genetic analysis await ethics committee approval. After a child develops meningitis and the community blames the researchers' photographs, the questions ask whether demographic data collection required approval, what safeguards isolated groups need, and what the investigators owe to children who fall ill during the study.

sections.title: Chapter II Issues in Study Design

summary.text: Introduces Chapter II on study design, starting with whether research ethics committees should judge the scientific quality of the protocols they review. It argues that a study too flawed to yield knowledge cannot justify burdens on participants, yet sound design alone does not make research ethical, and a less burdensome design may have to be weighed against lower scientific value. It considers who should carry out scientific review, favouring separate review where resources allow and suitable expertise on committees where they do not, before turning to specific design questions such as placebo controls. The chapter introduction ends with annotated suggested readings on topics including clinical equipoise and the use of mystery clients.

sections.title: Case 5. Referral of severely ill children to hospital

summary.text: Case 5 describes a prospective study in South-East Asia tracking how many severely ill children under five referred to hospital under IMCI guidelines actually reach care, with caregiver interviews at the first-level facility and follow-up home visits, offering help to reach hospital for those who have not. It asks whether the study poses an ethical dilemma and whether researchers' presence obliges them to offer assistance, including monetary help that would not last beyond the study.

sections.title: Case 6. Negotiating safe sex practices

summary.text: Case 6 describes an anthropologist's study in a west African country in which research associates posed as male clients to learn how women in the sex trade negotiate condom use, approved by the health ministry's ethics committee on condition that the women were paid for lost time. An international journal later judged the deception unethical, and the case asks whether the design was justified, what the committee could have advised, whether the journal should defer to the local approval, and how results could be shared with participants.

sections.title: Case 7. Investigating treatment recommendations

summary.text: Case 7 describes a planned study at a south Asian infectious-disease hospital in which young men posing as villagers would ask drug sellers for advice on treating a child's diarrhoea and buy what was recommended, without the sellers knowing or consenting. It asks whether sellers have a right to know they are studied, whether the investigator should intervene with those giving risky advice, how risks and community benefits compare, and whether all sellers should be debriefed.

sections.title: Case 8. Testing a new HBV vaccine

summary.text: Case 8 sets out the burden of chronic hepatitis B in developing countries and the shift from plasma-derived to recombinant vaccines because of safety concerns. It describes a randomized, double-blind trial in a large Asian country of a North American company's new recombinant vaccine, comparing it with plasma-derived vaccine and placebo in 240 infants of HBsAg-positive mothers, at a time when local vaccine coverage was below 20%. The questions ask whether a placebo arm was ethical, how the study could be improved, and whether consent from one parent was enough.

sections.title: Case 9. Tuberculosis prevention in HIV-positive people

summary.text: Case 9 explains that tuberculosis is a leading cause of death among people with HIV and that isoniazid was the standard preventive therapy for high-risk HIV-negative people, recommended in the United States for HIV-infected people but not then policy in developing countries. It describes a 1993–1995 randomized, placebo-controlled trial among 3000 HIV-positive African adults comparing placebo, six months of isoniazid and two shorter, costlier multi-drug regimens, with the placebo justified by doubts about safety and efficacy in HIV infection. The questions ask whether the placebo was justified, how it differs from no treatment, and whether testing an unaffordable regimen in Africa was appropriate.

sections.title: Case 10. Developing a vaccine for malaria

summary.text: Case 10 describes the burden of malaria, concentrated in tropical Africa and among children, and a planned efficacy trial of a North American university's multi-stage DNA vaccine in children under five in a sub-Saharan district with strong community surveillance but very few health services. Children would be randomly chosen from the surveillance database and given vaccine or placebo double-blind, with death as the endpoint, so investigators could not treat malaria cases even though nearly all deaths could cheaply be prevented. The questions cover whether a placebo is appropriate, whether to provide treatment, other duties of care, whether death is the right measure, how ethics should shape the design, and who must ensure local ethics review.

sections.title: Case 11. Should race be listed as a risk factor?

summary.text: Case 11 describes a southern African STI clinic director who, seeing twice as many STI cases among people self-identified as coloured as among those identified as black, plans a survey including race and ethnicity as risk factors on the hypothesis of biological susceptibility. A community member of the ethics committee objects that the findings would reinforce stigma and questions the biological basis, and the case asks whose view is right, whether politically constructed racial categories belong in science, and how the protocol could be strengthened.

sections.title: Case 12. Short-course AZT to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV

summary.text: Case 12 recounts the placebo-controlled trials of short-course zidovudine (AZT) to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission in sub-Saharan Africa and the Asia-Pacific, proposed because the long-course 076 regimen was seen as impractical and unaffordable there. Researchers defended the placebo as matching the local reality of no treatment and allowing faster adoption, while critics, mainly in the West, argued it breached the Declaration of Helsinki, whose placebo provisions are quoted in a footnote, and reflected a double standard. The questions ask whether donor-institution committees should insist on long-course controls, whether a likely less effective regimen should be tested, and whether a trial impossible in rich countries implies a double standard.

sections.title: Case 13. Testing an ayurvedic medicine for malaria

summary.text: Case 13 describes the retesting of Ayush-64, a patented combination of four Ayurvedic drugs used for decades against malaria in South Asia but never studied for toxicity and supported only by an older study without laboratory confirmation. In a randomized trial approved by the malaria research centre's ethics committee, adults with confirmed P. vivax malaria at periurban clinics received either the national chloroquine–primaquine regimen or Ayush-64, with non-responders switched to standard treatment and no follow-up of drop-outs; footnotes explain chloroquine, the malaria species, Ayurveda and primaquine. The questions ask what evidence is needed before human testing, whether traditional therapies should be treated differently, whether the study was ethical, and what was owed to drop-outs.

sections.title: Case 14. Evaluating the use of traditional medicines for diarrhoea

summary.text: Case 14 concerns 'ajorno', a cheap and popular South Asian traditional medicine based on the plant thankuni, reputed to treat bloody diarrhoea but never clinically studied and of unknown chemical composition. An investigator proposes a double-blind trial against norfloxacin, the effective but often unavailable and costly antibiotic for dysentery, but the ethics committee rejects it, citing unknown composition, vague prior reports and no peer-reviewed evidence. He accuses the committee of Western bias, and the questions ask whether the committee was right, whether the bias charge holds, whether approval would imply a double standard, and how such disagreements could be mediated.

sections.title: Case 15. Twin registry genetics

summary.text: Case 15 describes a European and South-East Asian population twin study of about 2000 twin pairs and 1000 singletons, examining genetic versus environmental causes and prevalence of common mental disorders, using interviews and cheek swabs to determine twin type, and excluding the illiterate and severely mentally ill. Participants needing treatment would be referred without follow-up, and relatives contacted for those at serious suicide risk, and the questions ask whether the exclusions are acceptable, whether referral alone meets researchers' obligations, and what is owed to twins of severely ill individuals.

sections.title: Case 16. Observing newborn care practices

summary.text: Case 16 of the WHO casebook on ethics in international health research describes an observational study of newborn care in an East Asian community with high neonatal mortality, in which field workers are told only to record practices, and one watches a mother prepare formula with unboiled river water, diluted too much. Questions ask whether the worker should intervene and when, whether the study could have been designed to avoid the dilemma, what investigators owe participants in observational studies, and whether visitors to the household need to give consent.

sections.title: Case 17. Compassionate intervention during an observational study

summary.text: Case 17 concerns a field worker in an observational newborn-care study in East Asia, instructed not to intervene, who is asked by a family to help an older child with a high fever who cannot easily be taken to a distant, poorly staffed health facility. The questions explore whether care outside a study's design can be ethically required, how observational researchers should respond to inadequate local health services, and how the field worker might balance compassion against the risk of many further requests.

sections.title: Chapter III Harm and Benefit

summary.text: Introduces Chapter III on harm and benefit, asking whether the risks and gains of research are fairly shared and how participants should be chosen when a study offers advantages. It discusses the difficult task research ethics committees face in weighing burdens on participants against benefits to others, especially in early-phase drug trials, and the role of independent data and safety monitoring boards in halting trials early. The section ends with suggested readings, including works on research with children, the export of tissue samples and research in poor countries.

sections.title: Case 18. Rotavirus vaccine

summary.text: Case 18 sets out the burden of rotavirus, which causes an estimated 527 000 deaths a year mostly among young children in low-income countries, and recounts how a rhesus rotavirus vaccine licensed in North America was withdrawn after reports linking it to intussusception. A developing country's ministry of health, weighing a 1 in 100 risk of rotavirus death against a 1 in 10 000 vaccine risk, asks a state-run company to produce the vaccine locally, but the manufacturer refuses to transfer the technology, leaving compulsory licensing under the TRIPS Agreement as a possible route. Questions ask whether the vaccine should be used where rotavirus kills many children, what level of risk is acceptable and who decides, and whether the manufacturer or the country has obligations regarding patent rights.

sections.title: Case 19. Pneumonia vaccine trial

summary.text: Case 19 describes an African trial of a European pneumococcal vaccine in 20 000 infants, which protected 90% of vaccinated children up to age 3, after which some scientists wanted to leave controls unvaccinated to study protection in older children and long-term safety, though all controls were vaccinated. Questions ask whether those scientists were right, whether parental consent could justify withholding the vaccine, and whether further tests in older children would be justified.

sections.title: Case 20. Early termination of a trial

summary.text: Case 20 describes a breast cancer recurrence-prevention trial in which the data safety monitoring board, seeing a strong but not statistically significant trend favouring the drug after three years, recommended stopping and offering it to all, which a leading patient organization criticised for leaving the drug's benefit uncertain. Questions ask whether the board should have acted on a trend, whether the ethics committee should have been involved, what role such boards should have, and when moral choices may override statistical significance.

sections.title: Case 21. Pregnancy in health research

summary.text: Case 21 describes a North American NGO's trial of a vaginal microbicide to prevent HIV in high-risk women, often sex workers, in four African countries and one South Asian country, which excluded pregnant women and required monthly pregnancy tests. Many participants paused for pregnancy and returned within three months, suggesting abortions, in countries where safe legal abortion is limited or unavailable to varying degrees. Questions ask what researchers and sponsors should now do, including whether to provide safe abortion or warn of the risk, and whether such studies should be done where safe abortion is not available; in the extracted text the closing part of the case appears before its opening.

sections.title: Case 22. Acting in the face of conflicting evidence

summary.text: Case 22 recounts the controversy over non-surgical sterilization using intrauterine quinacrine, given to about 104 500 women before reports of a cancer cluster and laboratory evidence of cell mutation led to suspension of the main programme. A small group of North American population-research scientists kept promoting the drug, pointing to its effectiveness, safety and maternal deaths avoided, and organized its distribution without further studies or approval for this purpose. The questions ask whether such use can be justified where maternal mortality is high, whether drugs not registered in the exporting country should be exported to developing countries, and whether the scientists' conduct was a form of misconduct.

sections.title: Chapter IV Voluntary Informed Consent

summary.text: Introduces Chapter IV on voluntary informed consent, tracing its origins to the Nuremberg Code and its later development in the Declaration of Helsinki and the CIOMS guidelines. It sets out the three core elements of valid consent: capacity to decide, voluntariness and enough understandable information. The text discusses how unfamiliar research concepts can limit adults' understanding, how offers of money or free care can undermine free choice for people with no other access to them, and how some minors are able to make competent decisions. It ends with annotated readings on community engagement and consent in settings such as a vaccine trial in rural Senegal and the International HapMap Project.

sections.title: Case 23. Testing high doses of vitamin A on children

summary.text: Case 23 describes a double-blind trial of periodic high-dose vitamin A against childhood diarrhoea and acute respiratory infections in a rural West African community, where the chief and council approve the study after a public meeting but parents decline to sign consent forms and the chief threatens to expel the field team if it insists. Questions ask whether individual informed consent is a universal principle or culturally bound, whether leaders may consent for the community, when individual consent is unnecessary, and how the team and funder should respond.

sections.extract: CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH ❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Voluntary Informed Consent The ministry of health of a West African country receives a grant from a foreign medical institute to collaborate with its investigators on a double-blind study designed to assess the effect of periodic high doses of vitamin A on the incidences of childhood diarrhoea and acute respiratory infections (ARI).

sections.title: Case 24. Breast cancer in South Asia

summary.text: Case 24 describes a proposed trial by North American researchers in a South Asian country comparing ovary removal plus tamoxifen with no adjuvant treatment in 350 premenopausal women after breast cancer surgery, which the researchers say could not be run with a placebo arm in the United States. The principal investigator plans to leave out alternative therapies and randomization from the consent process, arguing that paternalistic medical culture there makes expressing uncertainty unacceptable, and supports this with views from South Asian immigrants, women's union officials and local physicians. Questions ask whether cultural differences justify a different consent approach, whether the outside views strengthen the case, and whether running such a study in a poor country because rich countries would not accept it is justified.

sections.title: Case 25. Testing a microbicide

summary.text: Case 25 of this casebook on ethical issues in international health research, filed under voluntary informed consent, describes a planned phase II trial by a North American feminist non-profit organization of a non-contraceptive vaginal microbicide gel among 300 HIV-negative women at family planning clinics in an African country. Participants were to use the gel or a placebo for about a year, with monthly check-ups, treatment of STIs, HIV testing every three months with counselling and the option not to receive results, referral if infected, and modest compensation. The researchers chose not to seek consent from the women's partners, which a community health committee opposed as exposing women to abuse, and the questions cover partner consent and notification, how the committee can be heard, and withholding HIV test results.

sections.title: Case 26. A study to determine the value of postoperative radiotherapy

summary.text: Case 26 recounts an 11-year randomized study at a cancer hospital in East Asia, run without ethics review, comparing surgery alone with surgery plus radiotherapy for oesophageal cancer, in which patients were offered 'innovative therapy' but not told they were in an experiment because the investigators feared culturally rooted distrust of research. A North American journal published the favourable results together with a critical editorial that the authors were neither shown nor invited to answer, and the questions address the investigators' justification, harm to patients, judging past studies by today's standards and the journal's conduct.

sections.title: Case 27. Micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women

summary.text: Case 27 describes a community-randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 270 villages of a South Asian country with high poverty and illiteracy, testing whether a weekly low dose of vitamin A or beta-carotene given to married women of reproductive age reduces pregnancy-related death and illness and improves infant growth and survival. Permission came from district health officials, the study was announced by a village crier as a ministry of health initiative, and individual consent was taken only from women who became pregnant, some of whom also had detailed examinations and infant measurements. About three months in, some of the 45 000 enrolled women objected to taking a Western medicine rumoured to be ineffective, and the questions ask about the ethics of randomizing communities, the adequacy of consent and whether participants must understand randomization.

sections.title: Case 28. Breastfeeding and mother-to-child HIV transmission

summary.text: Case 28, based on research from the 1990s, describes a one-year study at a general hospital in a central African country of the risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding, in which both partners gave consent and HIV-positive women were counselled not to breastfeed and offered free infant formula, so that those who did and did not breastfeed formed non-random comparison groups. Children were tested for HIV up to 18 months and seen every two weeks at a clinic with free medicines. When one HIV-positive woman decided to breastfeed, her husband objected and threatened court action while wanting the family to remain in the study, and the questions cover partner consent, undue inducement, whether the study was needed, its risk-benefit ratio and the investigator's role.

sections.title: Case 29. Humanized mice

summary.text: Case 29 describes a South American university's work towards a dengue vaccine using immunodeficient mice whose immune systems were rebuilt with umbilical-cord blood donated anonymously by about 100 women, whose consent form did not make clear that the blood would be injected into mice. A year later one donor read about 'humanized mice', complained that she felt cheated and demanded that her samples be withdrawn, and the questions ask whether she was properly informed, whether her request was reasonable and what more the women should have been told.

sections.title: Case 30. Donations for stem-cell research

summary.text: Case 30 describes how, in a country that allows stem-cell research on embryos up to 14 days old, assisted-reproduction clinics use a single merged form for consent to treatment and to the donation of spare embryos, avoiding words such as donation, research and informed consent because of perceived patient sensitivities. The questions ask whether such terms may be left out, whether one form can cover both purposes, and whether consent can be given for studies not yet defined.

sections.title: Case 31. Researching health care practices and needs in an elderly population

summary.text: Case 31 describes a survey of health practices and needs among elderly members of a formerly nomadic Saharan community, run by a European university with a regional health district, in which researchers asked the household head's permission before interviewing older parents in private. When an 80-year-old man became unwell during a long interview, his son accused the team of making him ill, and the questions consider how this could have been avoided, whether the consent process met older people's needs, and whether ethics committees should have reviewed the survey questions.

sections.title: Chapter V Standard of Care

summary.text: Introduces Chapter V on the standard of care owed to control groups in randomized controlled trials, particularly in developing countries. It examines Article 32 of the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki, which requires new methods to be tested against the best proven current method except under specified conditions that permit placebo. The text contrasts a single global standard with readings based on the care available locally, noting that a strict global standard could rule out placebo-controlled trials of affordable alternatives in poor countries. It closes with suggested readings presenting differing views on uniform care requirements, double standards and the dispute over revisions to the Declaration.

sections.title: Case 32. Testing a new HIV vaccine

summary.text: Case 32, set in the 1990s, describes a northern European company's planned phase III placebo-controlled trial of an HIV vaccine among intravenous drug users in a South-East Asian country, with the company providing the vaccine, equipment, computers and vehicles, and seroconverters treated under ministry standards that excluded antiretroviral drugs. Consent was a two-stage process with tests of understanding, and the protocol was approved by several ethics review bodies. An AIDS activist group condemned the lack of state-of-the-art care, while the company argued that such care would be unsustainable and an unfair inducement, and the questions ask whether the study was ethical and consider compromise positions, other services for drug users, the company's gifts and whether a local sponsor would change the assessment.

sections.title: Case 33. Short-course antiretroviral therapy in pregnant women

summary.text: Case 33 describes a European institute's trial in southern Africa of a single-dose antiretroviral regimen to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission, whose results led WHO to endorse the drug, although later re-examination found Good Clinical Practice lapses that left too weak a basis for European licensing. An east African regulator first refused a licence because the drug was not licensed in its country of manufacture but later gave way to international pressure, and the questions ask about the relevance of the European view, other options for the regulator and WHO's role.

sections.title: Case 34. Use of quinacrine for non-surgical sterilization

summary.text: Case 34 examines decades of intrauterine use of quinacrine pellets for non-surgical female sterilization, promoted as cheap and simple and used in about 104 500 women in more than 20 countries, although never approved for this purpose anywhere. It traces research since the 1960s, cancer and mutagenicity concerns that led an NGO to withdraw and leading health organizations to advise against its use, and criticism by women's groups of experimentation without adequate toxicology data or informed choice. It ends with the halt of manufacture and distribution and asks whether double standards on drug safety in contraception can be justified and who should decide.

sections.title: Case 35. Investigation of vaginal microbicides

summary.text: Case 35 describes a foreign-funded randomized trial of a vaginal microbicide to prevent HIV in women at East African family-planning clinics, where patients normally pay for medicines and Pap smears are unavailable. Participants would receive free STI testing and treatment, yearly Pap smears and care for unrelated illnesses during the three-year trial, but the protocol does not state whether such care would continue afterwards. An ethics committee member fears this level of care may be an unfair inducement, while women excluded from earlier trials have complained of missing out, and the questions ask how to define unfair inducement and whether the study should go ahead in that country.

sections.title: Chapter VI Obligations to Participants and Communities

summary.text: Introduces Chapter VI on what researchers and sponsors owe to participants and host communities, describing research as a partnership whose obligations should be clear from the outset. It stresses that this matters most in countries with weak health systems, where a trial may be people's only chance of care and researchers may be expected to treat them. It lists possible obligations, such as care for people excluded from or leaving trials, compensation for injury, continued treatment after a study, help with unrelated illnesses and for family members, and access to results and proven products, and asks how far the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence should reach. Annotated readings at the end cover care and treatment in vaccine trials and whether post-trial provision of beneficial interventions should be mandatory in developing countries.

sections.title: Case 36. Observational study of cervical cancer

summary.text: Presents a case, based on 1970s research, of an observational study funded by a South Asian country's medical research council to learn which cervical dysplasias progress to cancer, in order to design national control guidelines. At eight busy government hospitals, mostly illiterate women gave verbal consent to Pap smears without being told their lesions might become cancerous or that treatment existed, and those with dysplasia were followed every three months until carcinoma in situ before referral to an overloaded cancer centre. The study continued after a published longitudinal study showed all dysplasia warranted treatment, 71 women developed cancer, nine with spread, none were treated afterwards, and the case raises questions about justification, post-study care, duties arising from diagnosis, interim review, stopping rules and publication.

sections.title: Case 37. Testing a malaria vaccine

summary.text: Presents a case in which a multinational company plans, with scientists from an east African country, a placebo-controlled trial of a new malaria vaccine in children under five in a village with intense year-round transmission. Mothers would be recruited at a maternal and child health clinic with busy nurses helping with translation and consent checked by a standard questionnaire, while infected children would receive chloroquine under national guidelines despite 60% local resistance. Health officials object that consent is inadequate given female literacy below 40% and ask for free vaccine for all the country's children for five years if it works, which the company calls excessive, and the case asks about the ethics, the consent process, treatment and duties to the wider population.

sections.title: Case 38. Mental health problems of survivors of mass violence

summary.text: Presents a case of a European university clinic treating mostly South-East Asian refugees, which plans a study of internally displaced people in the refugees' home country to develop a culturally specific diagnostic scale for post-traumatic stress disorder. The researchers, with little local experience or language, would use paid community health workers as interpreters and ethnographers, conduct anonymous one-hour home interviews about violence and trauma after verbal consent, and refer high-risk people to a government health centre visited by a psychiatrist one day a month. No services are offered and results go to the psychiatrist and ministry, and the case asks whether an ethics committee concerned about emotional upset should approve it, who benefits, whether CIOMS Guideline 5 on informing participants is met and whether referral care should be assessed or upgraded.

sections.title: Case 39. A longitudinal study of rotavirus incidence among young children

summary.text: Presents a case of a longitudinal, community-based study of rotavirus incidence among children under two in a densely populated, poor inner-city area of a West African city, designed by a local medical university with North American epidemiologists who fund it. A cohort of 150 infants recruited at a general hospital with oral, witnessed consent is followed for two years with cord blood, stool samples and home and monthly clinic visits. Participants receive free medical care for the child and family, antimalarial prophylaxis and transport money, all ending with the study, and the case asks how these benefits affect enrolment and outcomes, whether they should continue and whether investigators must ensure the ministry uses the findings.

sections.title: Case 40. Testing a vaccine for childhood cholera

summary.text: Presents a case of a South-East Asian research institute testing a new three-dose vaccine against Vibrio cholerae O139 in children under five in a rural area of about 75 000 people, where the government clinic lacks medicines and cholera cots and health spending is 5 US dollars per person a year. Because the comparison group receives a tetanus toxoid booster and is more likely to get cholera, the institute plans a free state-of-the-art treatment facility, although some propose upgrading the government clinic instead. As the institute relies on grants and fears an unaffordable long-term commitment, the case asks who should pay for continuing care, what messages should accompany vaccination and whether participants and other citizens should receive free vaccine if it works.

sections.title: Case 41. Impact of civil war on health systems

summary.text: Presents a case of health ministry researchers in a sub-Saharan African country studying how armed conflict affects the health system, using focus groups with internally displaced people and host community members and interviews with leaders, officials and aid agency staff. Camps are chosen by district officials, participants are recruited by self-appointed community leaders, results go to officials who must relay them, no compensation is given, and the case asks about leader-led recruitment, duties to share results and mixing displaced and host community members in one group.

sections.title: Case 42. Determining who constitutes the community

summary.text: Presents a case from a South Asian agricultural district where tribal people, mostly landless and living in outlying hamlets, are excluded from local power, and government health services have declined while private care is costly. A public-sector health company proposes hospital user charges, and a multilateral lender requires a participatory study in which focus group members are chosen by village committees and meet in the main village temple, finding willingness to pay if quality improves. During a gastroenteritis outbreak, field researchers meet angry tribal residents and find that under 10% of participants had tribal names, but the principal investigator dismisses their concerns, and the case asks about participant selection, who represents a community, duties toward minorities and the sponsors' obligations.

sections.title: Case 43. Evaluation research on a disability rehabilitation programme

summary.text: Presents a case from a poor South Asian democracy where a right-to-education law covers disabled children and a national programme funds voluntary organizations 100 US dollars a year per disabled child counted by the census. A paediatrician-evaluator finds a model district's programme efficient and popular, but a new probing survey reveals many severely disabled, bedridden children missed by the census who are malnourished and lack medical care or rehabilitation. The district collector urges him to stay quiet to protect the programme, the census and the budget, while the expert believes he must expose the systematic bias, and the case asks whether he should publish, whether ethics review was needed and who is at risk in health system evaluations.

sections.title: Case 44. Clinical benefits of an immune-modifying supplement in HIV therapy

summary.text: Presents a casebook case about a large US trial, funded by a drug company, of an immune-modifying drug added to standard HIV treatment, which an independent board stopped early after finding no clinical benefit. The company then claimed a positive effect, withheld the final data unless its own analyses were included and sought to approve publications, so the researchers published using about 95% of the data. The company sued the lead researcher's university, and the case asks who owns study data and whether sponsors may block publication of results.

sections.title: Case 45. Genetic research on an island population

summary.text: Case 45 describes a 2001 agreement between a European biotechnology firm and the government of a genetically homogeneous island nation of about 90 000 people with high diabetes rates, under which the firm would sample families with diabetes to search for disease genes. The company promised funding to the health ministry, a new research centre and a share of royalties, but community groups, the democracy movement and the churches objected to the lack of public debate, privacy protection and benefit guarantees and to the patenting of life forms, and the firm withdrew. The questions ask whether a population collectively owns its genetic heritage, how governments should negotiate such deals, how benefit-sharing can be judged fair, and whether a non-profit sponsor would change the ethical picture.

sections.title: Chapter VII Privacy and Confidentiality

summary.text: Opens the chapter on privacy and confidentiality in a casebook on ethical issues in international health research, contrasting privacy as an interest of individuals or groups with confidentiality as a professional duty. It outlines three kinds of privacy interest (control over access to information, over being observed, and over personal decisions) and notes that what counts as an intrusion differs between cultures. It explains why both tangible interests, such as employment or insurance, and intangible ones, such as dignity and the shaping of relationships, deserve protection, and how research ethics committees should weigh risks against the value of the knowledge sought. The section ends by warning that whole communities can be stigmatized by research findings or by disclosing study sites, followed by suggested readings on returning individual results and on data protection.

summary.text: Presents a case on a study in an Eastern European country, where many abortions still occur outside legal centres, designed to measure post-abortion complications and link them to the type of provider across 140 villages. Women are found through providers, community health workers and women's groups, give oral consent, and are interviewed at home with safeguards such as dummy interviews, a focus on general gynaecological health and artificial privacy. summary.text: Presents a case in which a Central American mental health institute, seeking to compare the cost and benefit of long-term community care services, told centres to obtain patients' consent to release confidential psychiatric records and to reimburse care only for those who signed. summary.text: Presents a case in which researchers plan to study a genetic link between brainwave patterns and alcoholism in 300 families of a North American indigenous tribe, offering payment, and many individuals want to take part. A tribal representative body urges the ethics committee to reject the study for lack of consultation, disregard for beliefs about the sacredness of blood and the risk of stigma, and the questions ask how the committee should weigh community and individual views.

summary.text: Presents a case in which social scientists, with hospital permission, use records to find women with positive Pap tests who did not return for results, visit them at home, give them their results and refer them directly to physicians. They justify this by the health benefits and the hospital's ownership of records, and the questions ask whether confidentiality is breached and how else the problem could have been approached.

summary.text: Presents a case set on a commercial farm in southern Africa, where mostly male migrant seasonal workers live in compounds with few women, and health promotion researchers returned for a follow-up survey after agreeing their role with management and workers. Mapping showed hidden sexual contact between migrant men and local women, and registration revealed that about 8% of workers were under 16, most of them local girls aged 8 to 15. The researchers feared these girls faced sexually transmitted infections including HIV and were missing school, and the questions ask whether they should inform management and what obligations they have to protect participants.

It describes how households are approached, how children give consent and are interviewed privately with a decoy questionnaire, contact details and compensation, and then asks whether privacy, safety and valid consent have been adequately addressed.

sections.title: Chapter VIII Professional Ethics

summary.text: Opens the chapter on professional ethics in a casebook on ethical issues in international health research, setting out what can fairly be expected of researchers, ethics committee members, sponsors and funders in terms of integrity and honesty. It focuses on two broad areas, conflicts of interest and scientific misconduct, defining a conflict of interest as a situation where personal gain could compromise duties to participants or to sound science, and separating this from the tension between patient care and good science. It explains how industry-funded research and scientists' financial ties to companies have made such conflicts widespread, and discusses concerns about commercial research ethics committees and fees charged by committees. The section closes with suggested readings on industry relationships, whistleblowing and cross-cultural views of scientific misconduct.

summary.text: Case 56 describes a manufacturer-sponsored trial comparing tablet, patch and injectable forms of a new hormonal contraceptive in women from two socioeconomic groups, with the company paying researchers' salaries, computers and a per-participant fee and giving volunteers a small payment. Questions ask about the appropriateness of these benefits, conflicts of interest, partner involvement in consent, infections acquired during the trial and the sponsor's obligations if the product fails.

summary.text: Case 57 describes an Asian drug company that, after a regulator refused approval of its antipsychotic over heart rhythm problems, contracts an overcrowded eastern European psychiatric hospital to test it, with doctors paid per recruited patient and local regulators not told of the earlier refusal. Questions cover risk-benefit, disclosure duties across countries, ensuring capacity to consent, possible misconduct, recruiters' conflicts of interest and post-trial access.

sections.title: Case 58. Budget reviews by research ethics committees

summary.text: Case 58 describes a research ethics committee at a South-East Asian medical school that refuses to review a large North American family planning study unless it sees the budget, while the North American university fears the school's 10% overhead could sway members who are also on the research team. Questions ask whether budget review belongs to an ethics committee, how any conflict of interest could be handled and how capacity-building benefits should be weighed.

sections.title: Case 59. Determining the workforce costs of the AIDS epidemic

summary.text: Case 59 describes a European university team, fully funded by a west African mining company, studying the cost of AIDS to the company's workforce in the hope of prompting prevention programmes. A trade union official warns that the company may instead dismiss HIV-positive workers or downsize, and the company refuses to give written assurances. After the findings show rising health care costs, the chief executive asks the team to recommend capping HIV insurance benefits, and questions ask how researchers should guard against misuse of their data and respond to such pressure.

sections.title: Case 60. Action research on involuntary resettlement

summary.text: Case 60 describes a small NGO in a South Asian city that partners with a research organization to study how relocation from slums to a distant colony has affected people's health, education and livelihoods. The ethics committee bars recruiting case-study participants from the NGO's clinic users for fear they would feel coerced, so the team runs a random household survey, but by identifying with the NGO it faces pressure to give direct help and participants expect services. Questions concern the committee's decision, how far to meet community expectations, effects on informed consent and the tension between action and research.

sections.title: Case 61. Victimizing the system or a victim of it?

summary.text: Case 61 describes a young research assistant who finds that a respected senior researcher altered data that contradicted their lab's hypothesis, and then uncovers a wider pattern of fabricated measurements and non-existent patients. Despite a colleague's warning that everyone will lose, she files a formal complaint, and an inquiry leads the researcher, a major grant earner, to plead guilty to falsifying a federal grant application after more than a decade of fraud. Questions ask whether his pleas for leniency are valid, how whistle-blowers should be treated and who should enforce scientific integrity.

sections.title: Case 62. Truth and consequences

summary.text: Case 62 describes six genetics graduate students who suspect their professor of faking data, confront her, and after months of hesitation over the risk to their own research report her to the university. An investigation finds falsified grant applications and pressure on students to hide unwanted results, and after the professor resigns most students must restart their projects, leave or face years of delay. Questions ask whether they should have reported, what would have happened had they stayed silent and how universities should protect whistle-blowers.

sections.title: Case 63. The curious career of Dr Taylor

summary.text: Case 63 describes a renowned nutrition researcher whose infant formula studies, involving hundreds of supposed babies, are found by an independent panel to have never been carried out, yet his university takes no action after he threatens to sue. He goes on to publish an implausible study of his own patented multivitamin and memory in older people, later supported only by an untraceable author in his own journal, and he retires to promote the product. Questions ask about the university's duties, whether an ethics committee may weigh a researcher's credibility, and the roles of government, professional societies and journals in addressing fraud.

sections.title: Case 64. Whose idea is it, anyway?

summary.text: Case 64 describes a Central American physician-scientist who, asked by an international funder to review a proposal, recognises it as a near copy of an unfunded protocol he wrote with co-investigators at his former institute in another country. The funder rejects the proposal but, after an internal review that never contacts him, finds only possible negligence and treats the protocol as public domain. Questions ask whether the matter was handled fairly, whether a different standard applied to a developing-country researcher, which ethical standards apply, and who owns research ideas and deserves authorship.

summary.text: The glossary of the Casebook on ethical issues in international health research, defining in alphabetical order the medical, research-design and ethics terms used in the book, mostly drawn from WHO publications with other sources cited. sections.title: Appendix

summary.text: The appendix of the Casebook reprints the general ethical principles from the CIOMS International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects, noting that other principles also offer useful frameworks. It sets out respect for persons, covering autonomy and protection of those with diminished autonomy, beneficence, including non-maleficence, and justice, understood mainly as fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research with special protection for vulnerable people. It adds that research should leave low-resource countries no worse off, respond to their health needs and use the least vulnerable participants necessary, and closes with the ISBN and a note that the publication came from a WHO Research Ethics Review Committee project with the University of Geneva.

narratives.fr: Photographie sépia d’une femme enveloppée d’un châle et d’un foulard, debout près d’un robinet extérieur d’où l’eau coule dans une grande jarre en terre.
narratives.ru: Фотография в тонах сепии: женщина, закутанная в шаль и платок, стоит у уличного водопроводного крана, из которого вода льётся в большой глиняный кувшин.

narratives.en: A sepia-toned photograph of a woman with windblown hair beside a young child wearing a fur-trimmed hat and fur coat.
narratives.ar: صورة فوتوغرافية بلون بنّي داكن لامرأة يتطاير شعرها مع الريح بجانب طفل صغير يرتدي قبعة ومعطفاً مزيّنين بالفرو.
narratives.zh: 一张棕褐色调照片：一名头发被风吹乱的女子，身旁是一个戴着毛边帽子、穿着毛皮外套的幼儿。
narratives.es: Fotografía en tono sepia de una mujer con el pelo agitado por el viento junto a un niño pequeño con un gorro ribeteado de piel y un abrigo de piel.
narratives.fr: Photographie sépia d’une femme aux cheveux ébouriffés par le vent à côté d’un jeune enfant portant un bonnet bordé de fourrure et un manteau de fourrure.
narratives.ru: Фотография в тонах сепии: женщина с растрёпанными ветром волосами рядом с маленьким ребёнком в шапке с меховой опушкой и меховой одежде.
